Seismic Hazards
The principal seismic hazards are surface rupture, ground shaking, ground failure, and seismically-induced inundation. Surface rupture occurs along fault zones where fault displacement intersects the ground surface. Displacement may either occur suddenly during an earthquake or it may occur slowly as the fault "creeps" over a long period of time.
Ground shaking resulting from earthquakes is measured in terms of acceleration, velocity, displacement, and the predominant period of repeated acceleration peaks. A calculation of ground shaking characteristics expected to result from the maximum credible earthquake in the project area showed acceleration to range from 
0.3g^*
 to 0.35g, and the fundamental period to range from 
4\frac{1}{2}
 to 
5\frac{1}{2}
 seconds.
The severity and effects of ground shaking on structures depends on several factors, including:
 Magnitude of the earthquake
 Depth of focus
 Distance from causative fault
 Duration of Shaking
 Local soil/groundwater conditions
 The relationship between the fundamental period of structure and the predominant period of ground vibration.
 Design of the building or structure
 Quality of workmanship and materials used during construction.
Because the period and maximum acceleration will vary with many factors, the largest earthquakes may not be the most important for any given structure or site. For this reason, important buildings, facilities and unusual structures should have a specific seismic analysis.
There are several types of seismically-induced ground failures, including lique-faction, earth lurches, lateral spreading and differential settlement. Most of the ground failures are associated with granular soils, soils which contain less than 50 percent clay and silt size particles. During earthquakes, find grained granular soils can be densified by seismically-induced vibrations and thus result in differential settlement. Where the ground surface is altered by differential settlement, foundations will be adversely affected.
Liquefaction is the phenomenon of a soil assuming the properties of a heavy liquid resulting from a loss of shear strength. The most important factors determining susceptibility to liquefaction are: grain size distribution, relative density, confining pressure, number of significant loading cycles, and maximum ground acceleration. Liquefaction is most likely to occur in water-saturated silts, sands, and gravels having low in-situ densities. Liquefaction can lead to vertical settlement and, where liquefied granular layers are continuous over a large area and crop out in open faces such as the Guadalupe River and Coyote Creek banks, overlying soil masses can move laterally, rocking structures situated on the ground above.
* 1.0
g = Acceleration due to gravity
